about: Quentovic (the wic on the Canche, at Visemarest by La Calotterie), written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/quentovic.md and the spine. One port. A draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what the sources do not show. The dossier's section 8 lists what must not be claimed and this file keeps to it: where ships lay and where toll, mint and street stood is not known (the sites are the game's assumption); only Gervold and Grippo are named officers; Gervold and Alcuin did not live here; the place was not destroyed in 842; no light burned at Boulogne before 811; no castle or count at Montreuil before about 900.
woven: Woven with Rotomagus, Parisius, Namnetis, Herio and Burdigala on 6 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways, quentovic.corbie_agent made real (Corbie's man, whom the Herio file named), beats of the other ports' stories placed here and of these stories there, and the port's cards (encounters/neustria_west_793.json) put on their sites. Nothing was taken out.

ports.summary: The king's wic on the Canche: with Dorestad one of the two sea gates of the Frankish realm, and the usual landing for the English bound for Francia and Rome. In 793 there is no wall and no count, only a long busy bank, a mint, abbey storehouses and the toll of the king's procurator, Abbot Gervold. A merchant comes for wine, quernstones and glass to sell over the water, for English wool, tin and lead coming back, and for news, because every letter between the two kingdoms passes this bank.
ports.seasons: The short crossing runs most of the year: bishops cross at Easter, pilgrims from Pentecost to Michaelmas, and a king's envoy has sailed home in December with a fair wind. New wine comes down after the vintage and the men of the wic go up to the fair of Saint Denis in October (?); in Lent the cell of Saint Josse feeds whoever is waiting on the wind, and on the saint's day in the dark of December his keepers show the shrine.

history.text: Theodore of Tarsus, on his way to be archbishop at Canterbury, falls sick at Quentovic and sails when he mends (668-669). About this year Judoc, a Breton king's son, dies a hermit near the river mouth.
Boniface crosses from Lundenwic in a small swift ship with great sails and lands at the mouth of the river called Cuent.
history.source: Willibald, Life of Boniface c. 5 (dossier 4); the year is the usual one for his second journey (?)

history.text: King Pippin's new deniers are struck here; coins had been struck at the wic since the sixth century.
King Charles frees the ships and carts of Saint-Germain-des-Pres from his toll at Wicus, Rouen, Amiens, Maastricht and Dorestad.
Gervold becomes abbot of Saint-Wandrille on the Seine. For many years he is procurator over the kingdom's trade, taking tributes and tolls in divers ports and cities, chiefly at Quentawich.
history.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 16 (ed. Loewenfeld 1886; our rendering)

history.text: King Charles, angered over a marriage refused, orders that no Englishman land in Gaul to trade. The abbey's history says Gervold's plea stopped the order; Alcuin writes that sailing is forbidden to merchants on both sides.
history.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 16; Alcuin, letter 7 (ed. Duemmler 1895). The sources disagree on whether the ban bit

history.text: About now the king entrusts the cell of Saint Josse to Alcuin, to give alms to pilgrims.
history.source: Lupus of Ferrieres, letter 11, with the editor's date (Desdevises du Dezert 1888) (?)

history.text: In the autumn Alcuin's priest Martin lies sick at Wicus, at Saint Josse. The same year the king's heavier penny is ordered to be taken in every place and market.
history.source: Alcuin, letter 25; synod of Frankfurt 794 c. 5 (chronicle_793.json 794-06-frankfurt-new-denier)

history.text: King Charles writes to King Offa: true pilgrims pass free, traders among them pay the toll; each king's merchants have the other's protection.
On the tenth of July a letter reaches Alcuin at Wicus.
In spring King Charles inspects the Channel coast, sets a fleet and posts guards against pirates, and keeps Easter at Saint-Riquier.
Archbishop Aethelheard of Canterbury, bound for Rome, is met at Saint Josse by Alcuin's man with a horse and Alcuin's own saddle.
On the fourteenth of June Abbot Gervold dies.
history.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 16 (dossier 3); 806 or 807 in the spine

history.text: The emperor comes to Boulogne, inspects the new fleet and has the old lighthouse relit.
Deniers with a ship on them are struck at Quentovic and at Dorestad, and at no other mint (812-814).
The emperor's own merchants go free of toll everywhere but Quentovic, Dorestad and the Alpine passes, where the tenth is taken.
A fleet of Northmen comes on the emporium suddenly at first light and so rages with plunder, captivity and killing that nothing is left in it but the buildings ransomed for a price.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 842 (ed. Waitz 1883; our rendering); Nithard IV.3; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle A under 839

history.text: Lupus, abbot of Ferrieres, wins back the cell of Saint Josse and asks King Aethelwulf of the West Saxons for lead for his church roof, to be landed at the vill of Stapulas.
history.source: Lupus of Ferrieres, letters 11, 13, 14 (Desdevises du Dezert 1888); 849 or 852 (?)

history.text: On the eleventh of May the bodies of Saint Wandrille and Saint Ansbert, carried from the Seine for fear of the Danes, reach Saint Peter's near the emporium and lie on its altar five days. That December or soon after, Grippo the prefect is caught by a storm on his way home from the kings of the English.
history.source: Miracula sancti Wandregisili cc. 2, 4, 15 (MGH SS XV.1)

history.text: The edict of Pitres: new pennies from ten mints only, Quentovic among them, and the mint of Rouen belongs to Quentovic by ancient custom. Death for selling arms or horses to Northmen.
history.source: Edict of Pitres c. 12 (chronicle_793.json 864-06-25-pitres); Wikipedia (fr) 'Edit de Pitres'

history.text: The saints' bodies lie at Saint Peter's again. A blind and lame boy and his fevered mother are healed.
Montreuil, on its hill a short way up the river, is first named. Danes are said to hold the port about now.
The monks of Saint Josse flee to England; the saint's relics go to Winchester.
Count Arnulf of Flanders takes Montreuil through a traitor and sends Herluin's wife and sons over the sea to King Athelstan; Herluin retakes it with Northmen.
Hugh Capet takes Montreuil, soon called his only sea port. About now the last known penny of Quentovic is struck.
Harold Godwinson, wrecked on the coast of Ponthieu, is held by Count Guy at Beaurain on the Canche.

eras.text: The quarrel of the two kings. English hulls are few and nervous, one lies under arrest with her wool going sour, and Frisians carry what the English may not. The toll is still a tenth, the mint is busy with the king's new heavy penny from 794, and it is a hungry year: the cell feeds a crowd at its gate. Every letter between Charles and Offa passes the toll house.

The peace. English wool, tin and cloaks come over again and pilgrims crowd the bank from Pentecost; the toll men open bundles looking for traders dressed as pilgrims. From 800 the king's guards watch the coast, in 806 the old abbot dies, and from 811 a light burns at Boulogne that a steersman can find the coast by.

The wic at its fullest: abbey houses along the street, ship pennies in every purse, the emperor's merchants paying the tenth here and nowhere else. From 834 the talk is of fleets on the Rhine. Nobody builds a wall.

After the dawn. Burnt plots between the houses that paid, fewer English names, a watch kept at the river mouth. The trade goes on: a prefect rules the port, the cell has monks again from about 849, and lead for a church roof is landed at Stapulas. In 858 the saints of the Seine come here as fugitives.

One of the king's ten mints, and striking more pennies than ever, while the port itself thins. Raiders come again and again (864, 881, 890, 894 (?)). People who can do so move up the river to the hill of Montreuil; about 898 Danes are said to hold the bank.

A landing below a castle. The counts of Montreuil hold the river and fight Flanders for it; the monks of Saint Josse are gone to England; the channel is harder each year. A few potters and one moneyer keep the old name, and pennies of Quentovic are still struck.
Grass over the street. Ships for the king of the Franks lie under Montreuil, and Wissant and Boulogne have the crossing. An old man will show you where the mint stood, for a cup of ale, and be wrong.

sites.name: The bank below the street
sites.see: A long reach of the Canche between reed marsh and a low rise of roofs. At the ebb the hulls sit on brown mud in a row, stems to the bank: broad Frisian ships, a tall-stemmed English one roped to a post with a guard asleep beside her, river barges from upstream. Planks run from deck to turf. Smoke lies along the roofs behind; curlews, the slap of rope on a mast, the smell of mud, tar and wet wool.
sites.source: Where boats lay is not known (dossier 1, 8): the riverbank landing is the game's assumption, as in ports_793.json. Anchors and ship timbers came out of the peat at Visemarest about 1789 (Wikipedia fr 'La Calotterie'). The bar that dries and the wait for the flood are the game's (unlock_pilot_canche); the tide's range is large (?).

sites.name: The procurator's toll house
sites.see: A timber hall at the head of the bank with its doors open to the water, so that nothing is carried up unseen. Inside, a long table, a balance hung from a beam, tally sticks in bundles, and a clerk with wax tablets who does not look up at once. Bales stand opened along the wall. When the abbot is here there is a boy with his staff at the door and the place is quiet.
sites.source: The toll and its procurator: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 16; the tenth: Praeceptum negotiatorum 828. Where the toll was taken is not known: the hall is assumed (?). The rate in 793 is assumed to be the tenth.

sites.name: The mint
sites.see: A low house with a guarded door and no window on the street side. A charcoal hearth, a row of crucibles, a block with a die set in it and a man who strikes without looking, another who weighs each blank. Foreign silver goes into the pot in handfuls: broad English pennies, cut rings, a spoon. The ring of the hammer carries the length of the street.
sites.source: Coins struck here from the sixth century to about 980; deniers of Pippin; few of Charlemagne and Louis, many of Charles the Bald after 864 (Wikipedia en, de 'Quentovic'); ship deniers 812-814 (ship_classes_793.json). No Carolingian coin names its moneyer and the building is not found: both assumed (?).

sites.name: The long street
sites.see: A gravelled way running with the river, house ends and fenced yards on both sides, goods set out on boards and hides: wine casks on their sides, grey quernstones stacked like loaves, pottery bottles in straw, bolts of cloth, a tray of amber. Franks, Frisians and men the Franks call Saxons argue in three ways of speaking. Pigs underfoot, a smell of new bread and of the tanner.
sites.source: More than 35 ha occupied (Wikipedia fr 'Quentovic'); goods: wine, quernstones, cloth, pottery bottles and glass out, English wool, tin, lead and Baltic amber in, slaves (Wikipedia en, fr 'Quentovic'; dossier 4). The street's line is assumed (?). No fair is recorded here.

sites.name: The abbeys' houses
sites.see: A row of stout storehouses with locked doors and a cross cut in each lintel: Saint-Vaast, Saint-Riquier, Saint-Bertin, Saint-Germain, Saint-Wandrille, and later Ferrieres. Carts stand loading under the eaves. A monk in a travel-stained cowl counts casks against a tablet, and his goods go down to the bank past the toll house without stopping.
sites.source: Abbey houses or stores at Quentovic: Saint-Vaast, Saint-Riquier, Saint-Bertin, Saint-Germain-des-Pres, Saint-Wandrille, Ferrieres (Wikipedia en, fr 'Quentovic'); Saint-Germain's freedom from toll, 779 (D.122). That they stood in a row is assumed (?).

sites.name: Saint Peter's
sites.see: A timber church with a shingled roof a little apart from the houses, Saint-Wandrille's own. A plain altar under a small east window, a lamp, a gospel book chained in its box, a warden with a bunch of keys. Seamen's gifts hang by the door: a wax candle as long as a man, a silver penny nailed to a beam.
sites.source: The church of Saint Peter 'near the emporium of Quentovic', Saint-Wandrille's property, with wardens (custodes) and countless clergy and lay folk in 858 (Miracula sancti Wandregisili c. 2). That it stood in 793, and what it was built of, are assumed (?). Vows paid after a storm: Grippo (c. 15).

sites.name: The cell of Saint Josse
sites.see: A league down the same bank, a small church and a guest hall inside a fence, with the hill and the dunes behind and the river mouth shining beyond. Pilgrims sit along the south wall with their staffs and bundles, waiting for a ship or a horse. A monk brings round a pot of pulses. In the church the saint lies whole, and his keepers cut his hair when it grows.
sites.source: The cella sancti Iudoci, 'at Wicus, at Saint Josse' (Alcuin, letter 25); given to Alcuin 'to give alms to pilgrims' (Lupus, letter 11); care of those from over the sea and other poor, and its fish, cheese, pulses and wax (Lupus, letters 43, 71); a league from the port (Wikipedia fr 'Quentovic'); the uncorrupt body and the hair (Wikipedia en 'Judoc').

sites.name: Wulfgifu's house
sites.see: A long house near the bank with a bush tied over the door and benches down both walls: the ale-house where the men from over the sea lodge. A fire in the middle of the floor, a cask on trestles, a woman who is told everything. English is spoken at one end and Frankish at the other, and in the middle a Frisian is selling something to both.
sites.source: invented: a host among the English ('Saxon') and Frisian merchants of the wic (Wikipedia en 'Quentovic'); the host who answers for a guest is the Kentish law's (npc_text_encounters.md 1.1). The house is one of those that could buy off the raiders of 842 or not (Annales Bertiniani).

sites.name: The craftsmen's yards
sites.see: Behind the street, a scatter of sheds and pits in their own smoke. A potter's kiln with bottles drying on a plank; a woman at an upright loom in a doorway; a comb-maker sawing antler into plates; a man winding a green glass bead on an iron. Bone and horn cores lie in heaps. Everything here is for sale before it is finished.
sites.source: The dig on the Chemin de Visemarais, 2009: over a thousand early medieval features, waste from pottery-making, cloth-working, glass, metal, bone and antler (Wikipedia de 'Quentovic'); pottery into the tenth century (Wikipedia en).

sites.name: The slip in the reeds
sites.see: Upstream of the last house, a bank cut back to firm ground with a keel laid on blocks and oak planks stacked to season. Two men drive rivets in turn, a boy heats tar, an old anchor lies half sunk in the peat where somebody left it. Chips of oak float away on the ebb.
sites.source: No yard is recorded (?): assumed from the ships the port needed and from story/ships_793.json, which builds the small boat, the coaster and the sea-going trader here. The anchors and ship timbers in the peat: Wikipedia fr 'La Calotterie'.

sites.name: The pens on the river meadow
sites.see: Hurdled pens on the wet meadow behind the houses, full of small dark cattle and sheep brought down from the chalk. Herdsmen lean on the rails; a butcher works under a lean-to with his sleeves rolled. Hides are pegged out to dry. It smells of dung and blood, and the wind blows it towards the church.
sites.source: 30,000 animal bones from the 2009 dig, mostly cattle and sheep or goat, with no sea fishing on any scale (Wikipedia de 'Quentovic'): the wic ate meat brought in on the hoof.

sites.name: The strand at Stapulas
sites.see: On the north shore near the river's mouth, a firm strand below a farmstead and a storehouse, with the wide sands and the sea opening beyond. A ship lies aground at the ebb with grey pigs of lead being swung out of her onto a sledge. A monk with a tablet waits beside two ox carts. Wind, gulls, and sand in everything.
sites.source: The villa Stapulas (Etaples), first named in 849 or 852 (?) as the landing for English lead (Lupus of Ferrieres, letter 14); the name means a store (Wikipedia fr 'Etaples'). It is a vill, not a town.

people.name: Gervold
people.trait: A king's officer more than a monk: the procurator who takes the tolls of the Channel ports, King Offa's friend, by his own monks' account no great scholar, a fine singer and a builder.
people.want: The two kings at peace so the tolls flow again; English lead for the roofs of his abbey's churches.
people.fear: The king hearing that the tolls are short, or that his friendship with Offa was worth more to him than his office.
people.voice: Smooth and exact; names sums and saints in the same breath; never says no at once.
people.looks: About fifty-five, portly, tonsured, a fine dark cowl with a silver cross, an abbot's staff carried by a boy, a seal on a cord and a clerk with tablets at his elbow.
knows: what the king has ordered about English ships, and what he will order next
who goes free of the tenth and by whose charter
what King Offa wants, in Offa's own words
the price of lead on both sides of the water
when he will next be here and not on the Seine

ties.note: the same person
his clerk, who keeps the tablets here when the abbot is at Saint-Wandrille
Saint-Germain's charter takes the tenth out of his hand, and the monk enjoys it
they write to each other while the ports are shut
each is spoken of as the man to make the peace with Offa; Alcuin holds the cell downriver
lets Alcuin's letter-carrier cross free
the cellarer of Saint-Wandrille answers to him as abbot and counts what the toll sends home (?)
passes the cell's wax and fish without the tenth, and expects to be prayed for by name
holds the Englishman's ship because the king's order says so, and has his crew fed because nothing says he may not
his man at the river gate on the Seine: slow, honest, and the one tally the abbot never reads twice

lines.greet: You are a Frisian from Dorestat, which is good. The king takes a tenth here, and Saint Peter thanks you for it. My clerk will count, and I will listen.
lines.greet_again: It is the same boat, and there was nothing hidden in her the last time, which is the kind of thing I remember. Sit down and tell me what they are saying on the Thames.
rumour: The king of the Mercians wants black stones cut to the old length. Our king wants cloaks cut likewise. Between them a man could make a living.
I have two churches roofed in lead and a third in hope. The lead lies under an English hill, and I may not lawfully fetch it.
The king will be on this coast before long, looking at ships, and when he looks at a thing, it changes. Have your tallies straight.
lines.saying: A toll is like the tide. Curse it if you like, but be on the bank when it turns.
lines.to_heir: Your father carried a letter for me once and did not ask what was in it. I hope he taught you that.
lines.farewell: Go with God and the ebb. If the reeve at Lundenwic asks after me, say I sing as badly as ever. He will know it is not true.

people.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 16 (c. 12 in later editions; ed. Loewenfeld 1886): chaplain to Queen Bertrada, bishop of Evreux, abbot 787-806, procurator 'chiefly in Quentawich', envoy to Offa, 'not much learned in other letters' but a fine singer, roofed two churches with lead. His seat is the abbey, not the port: he is here on his rounds. No text has him buying English lead: that want is the spine's (?). His birth year is a guess (?).

people.name: Hildric
people.trait: Keeps two tallies, one on wax for the king and one in his head for the abbot, and has never yet confused them.
people.want: A quiet ship with a master who does not talk, for letters that must cross while the ban stands; in time, the toll in his own name.
people.fear: The day two strangers ride in with the king's writ and ask to see the tablets.
people.voice: Counts aloud under his breath. Answers a question with the number first and the reason after, if at all.
people.looks: About thirty, thin, tonsured, ink-black fingers, a plain undyed tunic with a clerk's short cape, a stylus behind his ear and a board of wax tablets hung at his belt.
knows: what every hull on the bank declared, and what she carried
which abbeys' men go free and whose letter is a forgery
when the abbot is expected
which masters can be trusted with a sealed thing
what the toll took last moon, to the penny

ties.note: the abbot's clerk; after 806 he serves whoever holds the toll, and knows more than they do
the toll counts pennies by tale and the mint by weight, and the two sums never agree
she tells him who lodges with her; he looks away from her ale measure
he put the seal on the Englishman's ship by the king's order, and the Englishman takes it as his own doing
writes the abbot's letters to the wic-reeve and adds a line of his own
passes the monk's letter case unopened, by the abbot's word
the Seine toll is the same office and a softer hand; they compare takings every Michaelmas
reads Saint-Germain's letter of freedom through every season and has not found the slip yet
sends the abbey's cellarer the tallies of what the toll owes the house, and gets back a cheese and a correction
from 814 Corbie's man on the row sends something south by every boat for the bay; the clerk has not been told what

lines.greet: She is six hundred and sixty weight, with four men, out of Dorestat, and you need not tell me so, because I can see how she sits. It is a tenth, so what is under the hides?
lines.greet_again: It is you. The last time there were eleven casks declared and eleven found, and I wrote it down, because that is rarer than you think.
rumour: The English keel by the post has been there since before Lent. Her wool is the king's now, in law. In fact it is the moths'.
Since the letter, every Englishman with a bundle is a pilgrim. I open the bundle all the same, because pilgrims do not carry forty cloaks.
Saint-Germain's man went through with thirty casks and paid nothing. His letter is good, and I have read it more often than he has.
lines.saying: Honest men and thieves pay the same tenth, except that the thieves pay it twice.
lines.to_heir: Your father's name is on my oldest tablet, and I never smoothed it out. Declare as he did, and you and I shall not quarrel.
lines.farewell: Go on your way. If you pass Lundenwic, I may have a thing for the reeve there, small and sealed, so ask me before you load.

people.source: invented: the spine's clerk of Gervold's toll house (black_stones hook; chain_black_stones 'npc clerk'). Hild- and -ric are Frankish name parts (Design/content/peoples/frankish.md 7). The toll-takers of the procurator are in the Gesta; none is named.

people.name: Gerwin
people.trait: Trusts nothing he has not weighed, and that includes the weather, the abbot and his own son.
people.want: Every foreign penny on the Channel in his pot and not in a hole in somebody's floor; a die of his own cutting that the king would notice.
people.fear: A light penny with this mint's name on it, and the law of the new coin, which fines the man who struck it.
people.voice: Says a weight, then a loss, then waits. Speaks of coins as if they were people of doubtful family.
people.looks: About forty-five, short and thick in the arm, cropped grey hair, a scorched leather apron over a wool tunic, a small hand balance in a pouch and burn scars on both wrists.
knows: what English, old Frankish and cut silver are worth today, less his cut
which pennies are passing light, and from which mint
what the king has ordered about the coin
who has brought in a great deal of silver lately
how to tell good silver by the ring and the file

ties.note: the clerk counts, the moneyer weighs, and each thinks the other is guessing
changes her guests' English pennies at a kinder cut, and drinks the difference
the Dorestad moneyer; each says the other's pennies run light and keeps one in a pouch to prove it
his sister's son strikes at Rouen, with dies sent from here (?)
they have never met, and know each other's work by the weight

lines.greet: Put it on the pan, all of it. I will tell you what it is and then what it is worth, and those are not the same thing.
lines.greet_again: Your silver was honest the last time, or most of it was. Sort it before you bring it, and my cut will be smaller.
rumour: The English king's new penny is broad and heavy, and it is good silver. It goes into my pot like any other and comes out with our king's name on it.
After the harvest the old pennies will pass nowhere. People bring them to me in stockings, and some of those pennies have not seen daylight since Pippin.
A man came through with silver stamped in a writing like worm tracks, and it was finer than ours. I would give a good deal to know who struck it.
lines.saying: A penny has two faces, and so has the man who hands it over.
lines.to_heir: Your father brought me the first strange coin I ever melted. I have been sorry since that I melted it.
lines.farewell: Count them again outside, not because I am a thief, but because you should.

people.source: invented: no Carolingian coin of Quentovic names its moneyer (dossier 3). Ger- and -win are Frankish name parts. The heavy denier and the order of 794: chronicle_793.json 794-06-frankfurt-new-denier; Offa's heavy penny: 793-offa-heavy-penny. The link of Rouen's mint to Quentovic is recorded for 864, not 793 (?).

people.name: Wulfgifu
people.trait: A Kentish woman, widow of a Frankish wine man, who answers to the toll for every guest under her roof and so makes it her business to know them.
people.want: Her cousin's ship freed before the wool is past saving; the ports open; her daughter kept from marrying a sailor.
people.fear: A guest who does a wrong and leaves her to answer for it; a third winter with no English keels.
people.voice: Quick and plain, in Frankish with the English way of ending a word. Asks where you have come from and already knows.
people.looks: Near forty, tall, a linen head-cloth, a blue wool gown pinned at the throat with one small round silver brooch, a bunch of keys and a little knife on her girdle, a ladle in her hand.
knows: who has come over the water this week and what they said
which masters are hiring and which crew were put ashore
what wool, wine and quernstones fetch on the Kentish side
who among her guests is a pilgrim and who has a bundle
where a letter can be left and who will carry it

ties.note: her mother's sister's son; she feeds his crew on credit while the ship lies sealed
pilgrims who can pay come up to her; those who cannot she sends down to him with a loaf
he wants the names of her guests; she gives him some of them
he changes her guests' pennies and she keeps his cup full
the wic-reeve let her husband's last cargo land at Lundenwic when the ban was new
the Dorestad skipper drinks here, pays well and tells her nothing true
her brother keeps a boat on the strand at Dofras and sends his passengers to her door
she did not live to see him: her granddaughter's house, bought off in 842, lodges the prefect's men, and he pays for them

lines.greet: Sit by the fire. You came in on the morning flood with four men, from the Rhine, so you will have ale first, and then you can tell me what Dorestat is saying.
lines.greet_again: Your bench is free. I kept the knife that your crewman left behind, and it is on the beam. What is the news from over the water?
rumour: My cousin's wool has lain sealed on the bank since before Lent. If you have the abbot's ear, he has a ship and a long memory.
Three pilgrims came over yesterday, and one of them walks like a man with forty cloaks under his own, so the clerk will have him.
The reeve at Lundenwic is not a hard man but a frightened one. Bring him a gift and a story, and you may land.
lines.saying: Three nights a guest, and after that he is mine to answer for. So I count nights.
lines.to_heir: You have your father's way of sitting where he can see the door. He owed me nothing, and you should start as he ended.
lines.farewell: Mind the bar on the way out, and if you touch at Dofras, tell my brother his sister is not dead.

people.source: invented: English merchants lived at the wic (Wikipedia en 'Quentovic'). Wulf- and -gifu are English name parts (npc_text_encounters.md 1.3). The host who answers for a guest kept three nights: laws of Hlothhere and Eadric (wording to check (?)). Women trading in their own names are not attested among the Franks (peoples/frankish.md 5): she keeps a house, not a ship.

people.name: Osmund
people.trait: A Northumbrian monk who keeps Alcuin's hospice: patient with the poor, short with the proud, and homesick for a library he last saw at York.
people.want: Wax, fish and pulses enough for whoever is at the gate; a book to read aloud in Lent that he has not read aloud nine times.
people.fear: Turning away somebody who was Christ; a sickness in the guest hall with the house full.
people.voice: Slow and warm, with a schoolmaster's habit of asking you a question he knows the answer to.
people.looks: Nearing fifty, broad and stooped, tonsured, a patched black habit kilted up for work, a wooden ladle and a ring of two keys at his cord, bare red feet in sandals.
knows: who is waiting to cross, and for how long
what letters lie here for England and for the court
what the cell needs and will pay for: wax, fish, cheese, pulses
the lives of Saint Josse and of the bishops who passed this way
a Latin riddle or two, and who on the bank has more

ties.note: the cell is Alcuin's by the king's gift; Osmund keeps it for him and writes when the roof leaks
they were boys in the same school at York; Sigewine sleeps here whenever he waits on a ship
lodged the archbishop on his way to Rome and found him a mule
she sends him the pilgrims who cannot pay, and a loaf with each
they trade riddles across the fence and each believes he is ahead
the abbot passes the cell's wax and fish without the tenth
borrows books from the new school at Saint-Wandrille and is slow to send them back

lines.greet: Thanks be to God, and come in out of the wind. There are pulses in the pot and a place by the wall. Are you crossing, or are you carrying?
lines.greet_again: You are the Frisian with the small boat. The wax you brought burned on the altar until Candlemas. Sit down, because I have a question for you.
rumour: A brother from York is here with a letter case he will not put down. He wants a ship going north, and he is afraid of ships.
The harvest failed and they come to the gate by scores. I had a man swear he saw corn standing that was dust in his hand.
Our saint's hair still grows, and I cut it myself on his feast. You need not look at me like that, because you can come in December and hold the shears.
lines.saying: Every stranger is Christ until he has eaten, and after that he is only hungry again.
lines.to_heir: Your father gave alms here in a hungry year, and his name is in our book. We say it still.
lines.farewell: God give you a soft sea. If you see a library, look at it hard for me.

people.source: invented: the monk in charge of guests at the cella sancti Iudoci, which the king gave Alcuin 'to give alms to pilgrims' (Lupus, letter 11) and which cared for 'those from over the sea and other poor' (letter 71). Os- and -mund are English name parts. The porter's 'Thanks be to God' is the Rule of St Benedict c. 66. The false grain: chronicle_793.json 793-spring-false-grain.

people.name: Meginbert
people.trait: Saint-Germain's man at the wic: a monk who has not seen his cloister in four years, sells wine like a Frisian and collects riddles like a schoolboy.
people.want: A reliable carrier for the abbey's casks, so that he can go home; failing that, a riddle he cannot answer.
people.fear: The abbey's letter of freedom lost, burnt or doubted, and thirty years of tenths asked for at once.
people.voice: Cheerful and exact. Quotes Latin, then says it again plainly, then names a price.
people.looks: Mid thirties, round-faced, tonsured, a brown travelling cowl with wine stains at the hem, the abbey's sealed letter in a leather tube on his chest and a bundle of parchment leaves in his sleeve.
knows: what wine fetches here, at the fair of Saint Denis and over the water
which abbeys have houses on the row and what each ships
how the charter of 779 runs, word for word
the riddles of Aldhelm, and where the next leaf of a set is kept
who up the Seine will give a carrier the abbey's letter

ties.note: the cellarer of Saint-Germain-des-Pres sends him wine and orders, and no leave to come home
goes past the abbot's toll with a letter the abbot cannot refuse
the clerk has read his charter more often than he has, hoping for a slip
they trade riddles across the hospice fence
heard Alcuin set riddles to the king's son at court, and has copied them since (?)
buys the island's salt for the abbey's fish, and sent the next leaf of his riddles there
the Frisian carried the abbey's wine in a bad year, and reminds him
the salt brother of the island: Meginbert sent him the cask leaf, and gets back salt and an answer scratched on the sack stick
Corbie's man keeps his door shut and his voice down; Meginbert finds this suspicious in a seller of anything

lines.greet: A carrier at last, and God is good! I have thirty casks for the English side and a letter that takes them past the toll. Can your boat keep wine cool?
lines.greet_again: Here is my Frisian, who did not bring me one sour cask the last time. Sit down, because I have a leaf here that will annoy you for a week.
rumour: Wine is cheapest after the vintage and dearest at Saint John. The abbot at the toll knows that as well as I do, and he buys at Martinmas.
I have a riddle of Bishop Aldhelm's on a leaf: once water, full of fish, now white as snow. Twelve pennies, and it leads somewhere.
Carry three times for the abbey without loss, and the cellarer at Parisius will write you into our letter. Then the clerk may only watch.
lines.saying: The abbey's wine pays no toll and the abbey's monk pays for it in years.
lines.to_heir: Your father answered the salt riddle on this bench, after a week of bad temper. You look as stubborn.
lines.farewell: Keep the casks out of the sun and yourself out of the alehouse. One of those I mean.

people.source: invented: the spine's monk on his abbey's business with Aldhelm's salt riddle (riddle_road hook; riddles_793.json riddle_aldhelm_19_salis, 12 d). Megin- and -bert are Frankish name parts. Saint-Germain-des-Pres had a house here and freedom from the toll by the charter of 779 (D.122; unlocks_793.json unlock_charter_quentovic). Alcuin's riddle dialogue for Pippin, about 790: the spine.

people.name: Leofstan
people.trait: A Mercian shipmaster of Lundenwic who landed on the wrong day: his ship is sealed, his wool is spoiling, and he has decided to be patient out loud.
people.want: His ship back, or at least his wool sold before it is worth nothing; afterwards, a partner on the Frankish side who can be trusted.
people.fear: Going home to tell four families there is no share; his own king hearing that he begged a Frank.
people.voice: Loud, wry, counts days. Speaks Frankish badly on purpose and understands all of it.
people.looks: About thirty-five, big and fair, a sunburnt neck, a short English cloak pinned on the right shoulder, a seax across his belly and wool grease on his sleeves.
knows: what the ban really stops on the English side and what slips through
the Thames, the Wantsum and the bar of the Canche
what Kentish and Mercian wool fetches when it is not rotting
which reeves take a gift and which take offence
how long a crossing takes with the wind in each quarter

ties.note: his cousin, who feeds his crew and scolds him for landing
the clerk sealed his ship; he calls the clerk a name the clerk pretends not to know
only the abbot's word can free the ship, and the abbot has not said no
sails out of the wic-reeve's port and carried his messages before the ban
the Frisian offered a tenth of its worth for the wool, smiling
the wool is another man's until it is sold, and that man is counting too
no kin: a West Saxon wine buyer of the same name. Toll men on both rivers have charged each the other's debts, and neither finds it funny yet

lines.greet: Welcome to the bank. That is my ship by the post, with the Frank asleep on her, and she has lain there forty days. Ask me how the wool is.
lines.greet_again: Here is the Frisian, who is free to come and go, I see. I do not hold it against you, or not very much.
rumour: They say that Hamwic is half open, because the West Saxons never read a king's order that they could mislay, and I wish that I had gone there.
The reeve at Lundenwic turns Frankish hulls away with tears in his eyes and a hand held out. A Frisian is not a Frank, if he has a gift.
The crossing is one daylight with the wind west of south. I have done it between Mass and dark, and I could do it again tomorrow.
lines.saying: Wool keeps longer than a king's temper, and I am finding out by how much.
lines.to_heir: Your father spoke for my ship when no Frank would. Come to Lundenwic: there is a berth beside mine while I live.
lines.farewell: A fair wind to you. If you see my wife at Lundenwic, tell her that the ship is sound and that I am fat, and say nothing about the wool.

people.source: invented: the spine's English ship under arrest, her wool rotting (black_stones hook; chain_black_stones 'npc skipper', flag ch_black_stones_ship_freed). Leof- and -stan are English name parts. Whether the ban ever bit is disputed (Gesta c. 16 against Alcuin, letter 7): the game lets it bite on one ship. After 796 he crosses freely until his death.

people.name: Grippo
people.trait: The prefect of the emporium under King Charles the Bald, an illustrious man and the king's envoy to the kings of the English: a hard officer who made a vow in a storm and kept it.
people.want: The bank rebuilt and paying; no blade or horse sold to a Northman from his port; the saints of the Seine honoured while they shelter here.
people.fear: Another first light like the year of the three kings' war; the sea between here and Kent in December.
people.voice: Blunt, a soldier's Frankish. Speaks of the saints as a man speaks of a creditor he has paid.
people.looks: About fifty, grey and weathered, a long moustache, a red cloak with a gilt brooch over a mail-less leather coat, a sword in a tooled sheath and a small silver cross worn outside his shirt.
knows: what the king has ordered about coin, arms and horses
which sails have been seen off the river mouth this month
the crossing to Kent and the look of the light at Boulogne at dawn
who on the bank paid the raiders in his father's time and who could not
what the kings of the English want from the Franks

ties.note: her granddaughter's house was one of those ransomed in 842; his men lodge there now and he pays for them
the wardens who carry Saint Wandrille's body took his gifts on Christmas Eve and wrote his storm into their book
the king's officer on the West Saxon side, who saw him off in December
a Dane who holds a Frankish port by a king's gift is everything Grippo is set here to prevent
the clerk at Rouen sends him word of what passes up the Seine; the prefect sends back what the king will not do about it

lines.greet: Tell me whose ship she is, where she is from and what is in her, and then we can be friends. I am the king's prefect here, and the tenth is the king's.
lines.greet_again: You are of the house from Dorestat, whose people have been landing here since my grandfather's day. Declare what you carry, and then drink with me.
rumour: I was half over from Kent as the night ended, and the sea rose. At sunrise I saw the old tower on the shore and prayed, and the sea calmed.
The fathers of Saint Wandrille carry their abbot's bones from church to church, ahead of the Danes. The bones lay here for five days, and the whole bank wept.
Sell a Northman a sword or a horse from this port and it is your neck, by the king's law. I will not ask twice whose blade it is.
lines.saying: A vow made in a storm is a debt like any other. Pay it on the first dry day.
lines.to_heir: Your father's house paid its tenth in the year after the fire, when most men hid. I have not forgotten whose it was.
lines.farewell: Cross by daylight. And if the wind fails you, there is a saint or two on this coast who owes me a hearing.

people.source: Miracula sancti Wandregisili c. 15 (MGH SS XV.1): Grippo, 'prefect of the emporium of Quentovic', illuster vir, Charles the Bald's envoy 'to the kings of the English', 858 or soon after; the storm near dawn, the lighthouse on the shore 'built of old by the skill of the ancients' (Boulogne's, by inference), his prayer and the gifts paid on Christmas Eve. His years in office beyond 858 are a guess (?); the arms law is the edict of Pitres, 864. His looks and his temper are invented.

people.name: Theudold
people.trait: Corbie's man on the abbeys' row: a monk of the old abbot's training, who forwards what reaches him and has never once asked what was in it.
people.want: The old abbot home from his sand bar; until then, his letters across the kingdom and back without a king's man reading them.
people.fear: A stranger who knows too much about the abbey's business and smiles while he says it.
people.voice: Low and even; answers a question about letters with a question about wine.
people.looks: Near forty, tall, grave, tonsured, a clean black habit, a writing case on a strap and a small leather-wrapped book that is always just leaving his hands.
knows: which boats go to the Loire and the bay, and which masters keep a thing dry
the road from the Canche to the Somme and how long a letter takes
who at court speaks for the old abbot and who against
what the abbey buys at the wic: wax, tin, English cloth

ties.note: His abbot, exiled to the salt island from 814 to 821: Theudold is still his monk, whatever the emperor has written.
Saint-Germain's man two doors down sells louder and riddles in the street; Corbie's man thinks both unbecoming.
The clerk would like to know what leaves Corbie's house for the south, and has not been told.
Knew him as a boy in the school at Corbie, and sends him wax and news when he goes north (?).

lines.greet: From the bay? Then come inside and tell me about the salt, slowly, with the door shut.
lines.greet_again: You keep a thing dry and a mouth shut. The abbey has wine for such a man, and sometimes work.
rumour: The old abbot asks about bees and granaries in every letter, so the men who read them at court are very bored, which is the idea.
A boy of our school has gone to the new house in Saxony and talks of going on to the Danes. Remember the name Anskar, if you sail there.
lines.saying: A letter is safest in the pack of a man who cannot read it.
lines.farewell: Go by the bay if you go south. There is a guest house on an island there that is glad of visitors.

people.source: invented (Theud- + -old, attested Frankish name parts; names_placeholder.json), to give the Herio file's Adalard his tie and the story herio.emperors_cousin its agent. That Corbie kept a man at Quentovic is not attested: other abbeys (Saint-Germain, Saint-Wandrille, Ferrieres) held houses or rights there (?). Adalard's exile on Herio, 814-821, and Anskar's schooling at Corbie: the Herio file and the spine.

stories.title: A small thing, and sealed
stories.summary: While the two kings will not speak, their officers do: the abbot who takes the tolls here and the wic-reeve at Lundenwic write to each other, and somebody has to carry it. An English ship lies sealed on the bank with her wool going sour, and the abbot wants lead for a roof that the law will not let him fetch.
stories.picture: A clerk at the toll house door at dusk holding out a small sealed packet to a Frisian skipper, a roped English ship on the mud behind them with a guard asleep beside her.

beats.text: Leofstan's ship is roped to a post with the toll's seal on her hatch. He will tell anybody how many days. His cousin Wulfgifu feeds his crew and says the abbot has not said no.
Hildric wants a quiet ship for a letter to the wic-reeve Wighelm at Lundenwic. A Frisian is not an Englishman and not quite a Frank, which is the point. He pays on the answer.
Wighelm turns Frankish hulls away and lets a Frisian land for a gift and a story. He reads the letter twice and gives back an answer and a rod cut to a length: the stones the king wants.
The clerk breaks the seal behind the table. You may take his silver, or ask a favour instead: a word to the abbot for the sealed ship.

At Saint-Wandrille on the Seine, the abbot's own house, Offa's letters lie in a chest. A monk there says what the quarrel was about: not stones or cloaks, but a daughter asked for and a daughter asked back.
Lead from the hills behind Legacaestir, carried in a Frisian hull, is nobody's breach of the king's order. Gervold weighs the pigs himself and passes the cargo without the tenth.
After the king's letter of 796 true pilgrims pass free and traders pay. Hildric opens bundles on the bank looking for cloaks, and asks you which of your passengers is which.
Abbot Fardulf writes to the wic-reeve too, about ground at Lundenwic that the saint claims. He asks what the clerk on the Canche pays a quiet ship, and offers a little less.
The toll man at the Seine gate has passed six of the reeve's letters down to the abbot and read none. He says what the ban is, as far as a tollman is told.

endings.how: You carried the letters and asked for the Englishman's ship instead of silver.
endings.text: The seal comes off the hatch. Half the wool is saved. Leofstan sails on the next ebb and tells every English bank whose word freed him.
endings.reward: Leofstan a fast friend, and a berth beside his at Lundenwic; Wulfgifu's bench (quentovic.unlock.wulfgifus_bench); the chain's flag ch_black_stones_ship_freed.

endings.how: You carried the letters for pay and brought the abbot his lead.
endings.text: Gervold has a third roof and a Frisian he can use. The toll is light on you while he lives, and Hildric keeps your name on the good tablet.
endings.reward: Silver from the chain (the lead pays 160 d and no toll); the abbot's word (quentovic.unlock.abbots_word); the way to unlock_factor_quentovic.

endings.how: You opened the letter, or sold what was in it.
endings.text: A seal mended with a hot knife does not fool a clerk who reads seals for his living. You are paid by somebody else, and the toll house door is narrower for you after.
endings.reward: Silver now; Hildric wary for years; the English side learns what the Franks were offering (the chain's flag ch_black_stones_read or ch_black_stones_sold).

stories.reward: A friend on one side of the toll table or the other: the abbot's favour, or an English skipper who owes you his ship.

stories.title: The bag and the answer
stories.summary: At the cell of Saint Josse a Northumbrian monk waits with Alcuin's answer to the bishop of the holy island and a small bag of alms for the ransom of the boys who were carried off (?). He needs a ship going north, he is afraid of ships, and the bishop is old.
stories.picture: A tall stooping monk sitting against the south wall of a small timber church among pilgrims, a letter case clutched under one arm and a little sealed bag in his lap, looking at the sea.

beats.text: Osmund points out Sigewine, who has been here since the last moon turning ships down. He carries a letter from Alcuin for Bishop Higbald and a bag he will not put down. He apologises, and then asks exactly where you are bound.
In the guest hall Alcuin's priest Martin lies sick, left behind when his master rode on. Osmund asks for honey and wine for him, and Sigewine will not sail until the fever has turned.

The news of the island was thirteen days old here when it began. A priest of the place knows which Frisian ships go north in which month, and writes Sigewine's name into the next one's count if you cannot take him further.
Higbald counts on his fingers what is gone, and reads the letter standing. The bag is for buying the boys back, if anybody can say where they are.

Asulf, who deals in captives, remembers every lot. The English boys went east with a Svea, because Christians may not be sold south to the Franks. He will say with whom, for a price or for a Frankish blade.
Osmund wants to hear the end of it. He writes what you tell him on a tablet for Tours, and puts a name in the cell's book.

Adalsind knows the tall English monk with the letter case: he sleeps by her hearth on his way down to Saint-Wandrille and complains of the cold in two tongues. He left for the Canche at the last new moon.
Eadhelm, who was a boy at York with Sigewine, asks at once whether the bag reached the bishop. He has a letter of his own for the north, and no better news of the boys.

endings.how: You carried Sigewine and the bag north and put both into the bishop's hands.
endings.text: The letter is read aloud to the brethren. The alms go where the boys went. Sigewine is sick the whole way and thanks you at each end.
endings.reward: The deed carried_letters and the bishop's thanks; Sigewine a friend at five ports; a text from Alcuin's hand for the chest; the thread's flag lf_knows_boys.

endings.how: You followed the trail past the bishop to the dealer and bought a boy back with the bag and your own silver.
endings.text: One of them comes home, taller, with a Danish word for everything. Alcuin hears of it at Tours and writes your name in a letter that is still read.
endings.reward: The thread's flags lf_boy_found and lf_ransom_paid; great standing with the church on both sides of the sea; free lodging at Saint Josse for your house (quentovic.unlock.josse_bed).

endings.how: You took the monk aboard and went about your own trade first.
endings.text: The bishop died on the feast of Saint Urban in 803 with the letter unread. Sigewine does not reproach you. He reads it over the grave himself.
endings.reward: The passage money only; Osmund cool; Sigewine still greets you, which is worse.

endings.how: You carried the bag and not the monk, and the bag was light when it landed.
endings.text: Alms are counted at both ends. The cell hears, the toll hears, and for a year no monk on the Channel gives your boat a cargo.
endings.reward: The silver; standing lost with every abbey on the row.

stories.reward: A name in Alcuin's letters and in the cell's book, and a monk who meets you gladly in five ports.

stories.title: Once I was water
stories.summary: Saint-Germain's monk on the abbey row sells a leaf with Bishop Aldhelm's riddle of salt, and a cleric waiting to cross at the cell gives away an easier one about a ship. The salt leaf is the first of four, and the last pays at the fair of Saint Denis.
stories.picture: A round-faced monk on a cask outside a storehouse holding up a small parchment leaf between two fingers, a merchant frowning at it, wine casks and a loaded cart behind.

beats.text: Meginbert sells the leaf for twelve pennies: once water teeming with fish, tormented by fire, now most like snow. It is Latin; you need a reader aboard, or Osmund to read it out.

A cleric waiting on the wind for England scratches three lines on a wax tablet for nothing: daughter of a fair forest, crowded with companions, leaving no track. Answer it to him and he tells you today's prices up and down the bank.
The answer is salt, so the next leaf waits where salt is made: at the abbey's pans on the island. It speaks of the cups of Bacchus and a countryman's wedge.
A wine cask, so the third leaf is where the casks come from. It flowed from cracks in stone and is most like ice.
A glass cup, so the last leaf is with a dealer in Rhenish glass. Black outside, wrinkled, the delight of kings' feasts, and worthless unless crushed.
At the fair of Saint Denis, from the saint's day in October, the abbey's man hears all four answers in order and gives the prize.
After the monks leave the island the second leaf is behind a tally board in the salt shed at the Loire city. Its keeper cannot read it.

endings.how: You answered all four, salt to pepper, and said them at the fair.
endings.text: For three fairs nobody but your house sells pepper at Saint Denis. Meginbert tells the whole row that he taught you, which is not quite true.
endings.reward: riddles_793.json rw_right_pepper (the sole right to sell pepper at the fair, three years); the deed won_great_riddle.

endings.how: You answered the ship riddle at the cell and let the salt leaf lie.
endings.text: The cleric crosses on the next tide, pleased with himself. You know what everything on the bank costs today, and tomorrow you will not.
endings.reward: riddles_793.json rw_tip_quentovic (every price here sure for a day); the deed won_riddle.

endings.how: You bought the leaf and sold it to a schoolmaster up the Seine without answering it.
endings.text: A leaf of Aldhelm is worth more than twelve pennies to a school with no books. Meginbert hears and is offended for a season, then sells you another.
endings.reward: A small profit; the thread's flag bk_knows_worth; no pepper.

stories.reward: The pepper right at the fair of Saint Denis, or a day's sure prices at Quentovic.

stories.title: The king's name on it
stories.summary: This is the Channel mint: English pennies go into the pot and come out Frankish, less the moneyer's cut. From the harvest of 794 only the king's new heavy penny passes, and seventy years later this is one of the ten mints left in the kingdom, with Rouen's dies in its keeping.
stories.picture: A moneyer in a scorched apron tipping a pan of broad English pennies into a glowing crucible, a small balance in his other hand, new-struck coins bright on the block beside him.

beats.text: Gerwin weighs what you bring and names his loss. Silver that comes to him sorted, good from doubtful, costs you less; he remembers who sorts.

Since the order, Wulfgifu's English guests arrive with purses nobody on the street will take. She asks whether you will change them at better than the mint's cut, quietly, and carry the silver to Gerwin yourself.
Offa's new penny is broad and heavy. On the Strand a Frankish denier goes on the scale like any lump; here an English one does. Somebody who crosses often holds both and loses on neither.
Sigimar at the Rhine mint keeps a Quentovic penny in a pouch to show that it runs light. Gerwin keeps one of his. Each will pay to hear what the other said.
For two years the mint strikes a penny with a ship on it: a curved hull, a mast and stays. Only here and at Dorestad. The moneyer will set aside the first bright one for a house he trusts.
By the king's edict every old penny is dead at Martinmas and ten mints strike the new. The hammer here does not stop from dawn to dark, and the dies for Rouen go up the coast under guard.
Gerold strikes at the Seine with dies cut on the Canche. He sends his uncle word by any boat going north: the reverse die is cracking, and he has a coin on his tray that he cannot read.
On the Garonne a moneyer keeps a board of short pennies nailed up, three of them from the Seine. He will give a penny for a Quentovic one, to see whether the uncle strikes truer than the nephew.

endings.how: You brought silver sorted and fairly bought, year on year.
endings.text: The moneyer's cut on your silver falls to the least he may lawfully take, and he sends for you first when the coin changes.
endings.reward: quentovic.unlock.sorted_silver (a smaller loss at this mint for your house); the thread's flag sv_moneyer_trusts; a ship penny kept for you in 812.

endings.how: You changed the English guests' pennies yourself at the ale-house and took the cut.
endings.text: A good small trade until the clerk counts how little English silver reaches the mint. Wulfgifu thinks well of you; Gerwin does not, and says so on the street.
endings.reward: Silver each visit to 800; Wulfgifu's goodwill; Gerwin cool, and Hildric curious.

endings.how: You passed old or foreign coin at face in the market after the order.
endings.text: The fine for refusing the king's coin has a twin for passing any other. It is paid at the toll house, with Hildric writing.
endings.reward: Nothing gained: the thread's flag sv_old_coin and a fine.

stories.reward: The mint's trust and its smallest cut, and the first ship penny off the die.

stories.title: First light
stories.summary: In 842 a fleet came on the wic at dawn, and when it left nothing stood but the houses that had been bought off. The place was not destroyed: a prefect, a mint and the saints of the Seine all come after. What your house owns on the bank that morning, and what it does with its silver, is remembered for three generations.
stories.picture: A grey dawn over a river bank, long ships drawn up on the mud, smoke from some roofs and not others, a woman in a doorway holding out a bag of silver to a man with an axe.

beats.text: The talk on the benches is of Dorestad burnt, and burnt again. Nobody builds a wall. The heirs of Wulfgifu's house ask whether you would stand surety for them, if it came to buying off.

This year a fleet of Northmen came on the emporium suddenly at first light. If you have a house or a store here, word reaches you of what it would have cost to save it, and whether somebody paid for you.
Burnt plots between standing houses, like teeth. A wine man who lost his stock asks for a loan against next year's vintage. The ones who paid look at the ones who could not, and the other way.

A monk of Ferrieres has waited on the strand since Whitsun. His abbot holds the cell of Saint Josse again and has written to the king of the West Saxons for lead for a leaking painted church. Whoever lands it is paid on the spot.
On the eve of the Ascension the people go out with gospel books, crosses and candles to meet two dead abbots carried from the Seine, and walk ahead of them singing. They lie on the altar five days.
Grippo the prefect tells of his storm, and asks plainly whether there is a blade or a horse in your hold. He is looking for a house that was here before the fire and is here still.
A clerk of the cathedral who saw his own city burn in May gives every boat bound for the Canche the same word: they came on a feast, up the tide, and nobody had shut a gate.
At the Loire they ask what Quentovic paid to keep its houses standing. Nobody at Nantes was offered a price.

endings.how: You stood surety before 842, or paid the ransom of a house that was not yours.
endings.text: The ale-house stands. Its people say your house's name with their own at Saint Peter's, and their children do after them.
endings.reward: Free lodging and the first news on the bank for your heirs; long_friend_quentovic from the loan card; the thread's flag df_warned.

endings.how: You were elsewhere that dawn and came back with silver to lend.
endings.text: The wine man pays you back at the next vintage with a cask over. The bank fills again, thinner, and your stall is in the front row of it.
endings.reward: Forty pennies and a cask (long.quentovic.loan_back); a plot on the street at a burnt-ground price; Grippo's regard.

endings.how: You sold what you had on the bank and took your trade to the Seine or over the water.
endings.text: Nobody blames you aloud. In ninety years there is grass on the street, and you were only early.
endings.reward: Your silver whole; the thread's flag df_moved; no friend here for your heirs.

stories.reward: A house on the bank that remembers yours across three generations, or your silver safe somewhere else.

works.name: A house in the street of the men from over the sea
works.what: A small house with a fenced yard among the Frisians and English of the wic, with a locked chest and room for goods. A man of yours can live there the year round and buy wine after the vintage.
works.needs: To be known at the port (standing 20), and a factor to live in it (unlock_factor_quentovic) or a crewman you trust.
works.gives: Room for 20 units of goods; free lodging; a factor who buys in the cheap season and sends prices home by any ship. It can be burnt in 842 unless somebody pays for it.
works.picture: A small timber house end-on to a gravel street, a fenced yard with two casks and a handcart, a man in a Frisian cloak at the door with a key.
works.source: works_793.json factor_house (the shared work, its cost and yield); Frisian and English merchants living at Quentovic: Wikipedia (en) 'Quentovic'; the houses ransomed in 842: Annales Bertiniani.

works.name: A storehouse on the abbeys' row
works.what: A stout timber store with a locked door, built at the end of the row where the abbeys keep their wine and wax, on ground leased from Saint-Wandrille.
works.needs: The leave of the abbot of Saint-Wandrille or his clerk (Gervold or Hildric friendly), and a yearly render to Saint Peter's.
works.gives: A large dry store under lock at the port; goods kept there over winter do not spoil; the abbeys' men treat you as a neighbour and offer carrying first.
works.picture: A new timber storehouse at the end of a row of older ones, each with a cross cut over the door, a cart being unloaded into it.
works.source: works_793.json storehouse; the abbeys' houses and stores at Quentovic: Wikipedia (en, fr) 'Quentovic'. That a layman could lease ground among them is assumed (?).

works.name: Beds for the guest hall of Saint Josse
works.what: Twelve plank beds with straw and blankets, and a second hearth, for the hall where the cell lodges pilgrims and the poor from over the sea.
works.needs: Alms given at the cell at least once, and the guest master's goodwill.
works.gives: The deed gave_alms many times over; your house lodges free at the cell for good; letters for England are offered to you first; Alcuin, and after him the abbots who hold the cell, hear your name.
works.picture: A long low hall with plank beds down both walls and two fires, a monk with a ladle, pilgrims' staffs stacked by the door.
works.source: works_793.json hospice; the cell given to Alcuin 'to give alms to pilgrims' and its care of 'those from over the sea and other poor': Lupus of Ferrieres, letters 11 and 71.

works.name: A name in the book of Saint Josse
works.what: Your name and your dead written into the cell's book, to be read out among those the monks pray for, with wax for the lamp at the saint's body for a year.
works.needs: To be a Christian, or to have one of your house baptised.
works.gives: Standing with every churchman on the Channel; act:remember here steadies a grieving crew; when the monks flee to England in 903 the book goes with them, and your heirs are known at Winchester (?).
works.picture: A monk writing a line in an open book on a slanted desk under a small window, a merchant standing with his cap in his hands.
works.source: works_793.json book_of_life; what counts is alms, masses and a name in the monks' book of the dead (Design/content/peoples/frankish.md 9); the flight to England and the relics at Winchester in 903: Wikipedia (en) 'Judoc'. No such book of this cell survives (?).

works.name: A wooden cross on the road the saints came by
works.what: A tall oak cross set up by the road outside the wic, where the bodies of Saint Wandrille and Saint Ansbert were met by the people with candles.
works.needs: To have been at the port in the year the saints came, or to have made a vow at sea and kept it.
works.gives: A vow paid in sight of the whole bank: crew morale after a storm; the prefect and the wardens of Saint Peter's count your house among the faithful of the place.
works.picture: A plain tall wooden cross at a roadside in open country, fresh-cut, a few candles guttering at its foot, roofs and a river in the distance.
works.source: Miracula sancti Wandregisili c. 2-4: a wooden cross was set up where the bodies had rested by the bridge of the Authie; a second one here is the game's (?). Cost from works_793.json standing_cross, less because it is wood.

ships.note: Every house on the bank keeps one for the mud and the far shore. Forty pennies and no questions.
ships.picture: A short flat plank boat with one pair of oars lying on brown river mud beside a larger hull.

ships.how: built to order in six weeks, or bought used
ships.note: The lighter and ship's boat of the wic, for carrying out to hulls that cannot come up on a poor tide. The wrights at the slip build them between larger work.
ships.picture: A six-metre clinker boat with four oars on blocks at a reedy slip, a man tarring her seams.
ships.source: story/ships_793.json west_small_boat (built at Quentovic, 150 d); unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_west_small_boat

ships.how: built to order over a winter, or bought from an abbey's man
ships.note: The abbeys' own carrier: Saint-Wandrille, Saint-Riquier and the rest send wine and salt along the coast in boats of this kind and sell an old one when a new is ready.
ships.picture: A ten-metre beach boat with a single square sail furled, drawn up below a row of storehouses, casks being rolled aboard.
ships.source: story/ships_793.json coaster_minster_ship (built at Quentovic, 1200 d); abbey houses at the port: Wikipedia (en, fr) 'Quentovic'

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The ship on the port's own pennies of 812-814: a curved hull, a mast and stays. Oak comes down the Canche from the chalk country; the wright builds only for a house the bank knows, and the timber is paid in advance.
ships.picture: A fourteen-metre keeled trader half planked on the slip, her curved stem high against the reeds, a silver penny with the same ship on it held up beside her.
ships.source: story/ships_793.json north_sea_merchant_ship (built at Quentovic, 3000 d); unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_north_sea_merchant_ship; the ship deniers of Quentovic and Dorestad: Design/content/ships.md [Coins] (?)

sayings.text: A tenth here, a tenth at Quentovic, and they wonder that a man goes in by the back creeks.
sayings.source: story/sayings_793.json say.inv.c.tenth (invented in the period's manner; the king's toll at both ports was a tenth)

sayings.text: The abbot is not much learned in other letters, but he can read a tally.
sayings.source: invented, turning the abbey's own words on Gervold: 'not much learned in other letters' (Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium c. 16, our rendering)

sayings.text: Our saint has his hair cut oftener than the clerk does.
sayings.source: invented; Saint Josse's body was said not to decay, so his keepers went on cutting his hair (Wikipedia en 'Judoc')

sayings.text: The king asked what use a short cloak was: it will not cover him in bed, nor keep the rain off him riding. The Frisians went on selling them at the old price.
sayings.source: retold, not quoted, from Notker, Deeds of Charles I.34 (tr. Grant 1905); Notker wrote about 885, so the joke is told LATER than it is set

sayings.text: Every Englishman is a pilgrim until you open his bundle.
sayings.source: invented, from King Charles's letter to Offa, 796: traders who travel among the pilgrims must pay the toll (chronicle_793.json 796-spring-offa-letter)

sayings.text: Lead for the roof, wax for the altar, wine for the Mass: the church is a good customer and a slow one.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; Lupus's lead (letters 13, 14) and the cell's wax (letter 43)

sayings.text: A vow at sea is paid on the bank, or the sea remembers.
sayings.source: invented; Grippo promised gifts in the storm and paid them on Christmas Eve (Miracula sancti Wandregisili c. 15)

sayings.text: What has one foot, many ribs and its mouth in the middle, and feeds a town? The clerk says: nothing that has passed my table without paying.
sayings.source: a turn on the Exeter Book ship riddle (texts_793.json exeter_32_ship; Tupper 1910): the answer is a merchant ship. The clerk's reply is invented

easter_eggs.text: An old priest who says Mass at the cell some Sundays was once Alcuin's deacon Putul. He sailed home from York with Liudger and the Frisian merchants when they fled, twenty years back, and will say why they fled if asked, and who struck the blow.
easter_eggs.source: the spine's york_blood hook for Quentovic (before 805); Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.12 has Putul sent with Liudger. That he ended a priest in Gaul is the spine's (?)

easter_eggs.text: In spring 801 a servant waits at the cell with a horse and a saddle 'fitted out as the pastors of churches have it in this country': Alcuin's own, sent for the archbishop of Canterbury to ride to Rome on.
easter_eggs.source: Alcuin, letters 230 and 232 (ed. Duemmler 1895; our rendering)

easter_eggs.text: From 811 a light shows at night far up the coast to the north: the emperor has had the old eight-sided tower at Boulogne relit. Before that year it is a dark stump, and a steersman who says he steered by it is lying.
easter_eggs.source: Royal Frankish Annals 811 (chronicle_793.json 811-10-boulogne-lighthouse); Wikipedia (fr) 'Tour d'Odre'; riddles_793.json palette 'lighthouse'

easter_eggs.text: An old anchor lies half sunk in the peat by the slip, and nobody remembers whose it was. It is still there a thousand years on.
easter_eggs.source: anchors and ship timbers came out of the peat at Visemarest about 1789 (Wikipedia fr 'La Calotterie')

easter_eggs.text: A penny of this mint, struck in King Charles the Bald's name, turns up a long way from home: in a pot at Fecamp with four hundred and seventy more, and in a great hoard by a river in the north of England.
easter_eggs.source: the Fecamp hoard, about 980-985: 472 deniers and 27 half-deniers of Quentovic (hoards_793.json 'fecamp'; Wikipedia fr 'Tresor de Fecamp'); the Cuerdale hoard, about 903-910 (Wikipedia en)

easter_eggs.text: An English clerk at the ale-house, copying his king's annals, cannot spell the place and writes it nearer to his own archbishop's town. In time nobody at all will know where the wic stood.
easter_eggs.source: old translations of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle turn Cwantawic (839) into Canterbury; an 1886 editor put the wic at Wicquinghem; the site was found only in 1984-1991 (dossier 7)

easter_eggs.text: The butchers at the pens will sell you beef and mutton and laugh if you ask for sea fish. The cell's monks send fish to their mother house; the wic eats meat.
easter_eggs.source: 30,000 animal bones, mostly cattle and sheep or goat, with no sea fishing on any scale (Wikipedia de 'Quentovic'); the cell's fish: Lupus, letter 43

easter_eggs.text: In 1064 an English earl is wrecked on this coast and held by the count at Beaurain, a little way up the Canche. He comes down to the water once, under guard, and looks at it for a long time.
easter_eggs.source: Harold Godwinson and Count Guy of Ponthieu, 1064 (Wikipedia en 'Guy I, Count of Ponthieu')

unlocks.what: A host at Quentovic: a man of your house living at the port
unlocks.how: Be a friend of a host here (Wulfgifu or her heirs) and carry letters; then 120 d. Also won in the black stones chain.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_factor_quentovic: a factor who keeps stock, sells what you leave and sends prices home.

unlocks.what: The bar of the Canche by heart
unlocks.how: Hire the pilot at the bank on three calls and come through without touching, or sail it three times yourself, or be taught it over a winter by Leofstan.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_pilot_canche: no pilot's fee here and the bar passed as sure.

unlocks.what: Saint-Germain's freedom from the tenth at Quentovic
unlocks.how: Carry for the abbey three times without loss (Meginbert's casks count) and be known at Parisius or Rotomagus; the cellarer writes you into the abbey's letter.
unlocks.gives: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_charter_quentovic: 'show the charter' at the toll does toll none while you carry the abbey's goods.

unlocks.what: The freshest word on Quentovic's prices
unlocks.how: Answer the ship riddle (riddle_symphosius_13_navis) to the cleric waiting to cross at Saint Josse.
unlocks.gives: riddles_793.json rw_tip_quentovic: every good here is sure for today.

unlocks.what: The abbot's word at the toll
unlocks.how: Carry a sealed letter for Gervold or his clerk and deliver it unread, and bring him lead once.
unlocks.gives: toll eased at Quentovic while Gervold lives (to 806), and at Rotomagus, which is the same office; npc abbot feeling +15; Hildric keeps it up at half strength for your heir.

unlocks.how: Lodge three times, leave owing nothing, and either speak for Leofstan's ship or bring her true news from Dofras.
unlocks.gives: Lodging at the ale-house costs nothing; act:rumours here gives the newest word from over the water first; act:hire_crew finds English hands. Her daughter keeps the bench for your heir until 842.

unlocks.what: A bed at Saint Josse for your house
unlocks.how: Give alms at the cell in a hungry year, or pay for the guest hall's beds, or end the story of the alms bag well.
unlocks.gives: Free lodging and act:heal at the cell to 903; letters for England and for Tours are offered to you first (commissions that pay in silver and in the deed carried_letters).

unlocks.how: Bring Gerwin sorted silver on five calls and never a false piece.
unlocks.gives: The loss on changing foreign coin at this mint is halved for your house (trade_rules.json foreign_loss 0.1 becomes 0.05 here); the thread's flag sv_moneyer_trusts; his heir honours it.

unlocks.what: A ship penny, the first off the die
unlocks.how: Hold the moneyer's trust and call at the mint in 812, 813 or 814.
unlocks.gives: An heirloom for the chest that every later heir can show: a penny of Quentovic with your kind of ship on it. Shown at the slip, it takes a tenth off a new keel (?).
